newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angola's UNITA weakened by attack in diamond area.
newsitem.headline: Angola's UNITA weakened by attack in diamond area.

text.p: A strike by Angola's army into diamond-rich areas mainly held by the opposition UNITA could be the last blow to the once powerful rebel movement that fought a 20-year civil war, analysts say.

Western diplomats say UNITA was caught off guard when government troops began a raid from the east in the Lunda Norte province two weeks ago, and has been unable to defend its diamond wealth, worth up to $600 million annually.

The government, after a military build-up in the northern border town of Dundo, launched the strike two weeks ago, calling it a clean-up operation to flush out armed refugees from neighbouring former Zaire.
Western diplomats believe that was a pretext by the government to reclaim land from UNITA, reluctant to give up its diamonds.

"The government is feeling quite victorious at the moment," one Western diplomat said. "They were successful in grabbing quite a bit of land in the northeast and they were encouraged by that. They see that UNITA is off balance at the moment and they are taking advantage of it."

Several foreign mining companies said they had suspended operations in Lunda Norte because of the instability. Diamond giant De Beers said it had temporarily closed one buying office in the province at Cafunfu.

UNITA's fighting power has eroded since the implementation of a 1994 peace agreement with the ruling MPLA, in which it agreed to dismantle its army and hand over weapons to the United Nations overseeing the transition to peace.

The fall of Zaire's Mobutu Sese Seko government to rebel leader Laurent Kabila in May was one of the biggest blows to UNITA, who used Zaire as its weapons and food supplies base throughout the 20-year war.

A foreign military analyst, who told Reuters UNITA had now moved bases to Congo and Gabon, said at the insistence of French advisors UNITA had helped to prop up the Mobutu army with some of its best troops during that seven-month war.
The analyst in Luanda said UNITA could have put up a fight for the diamond area but many of its troops were still returning from Zaire.
"The FAA (Angolan Armed Forces) caught UNITA off guard. Had many of their best troops not been in Zaire the fighting would have been much more intense," the analyst said.
The attack has gone unreported in media in the capital Luanda, in spite of civilian casualties reported by UNITA.

The government and UNITA were joined in a government of unity in April this year as part of the peace plan. UNITA fighters were incorporated into a single national army, while others were demobilised from U.N. assembly camps.
But U.N. figures show over 25,000 UNITA troops have deserted the camps, many since the raid in the Lundas began.

The government's actions threaten Angola's longest peace, although UNITA representatives in the new government have remained subdued. U.N. special envoy to Angola, Alioune Blondin Beye, worried about repercussions, met with President Jose Eduardo dos Santos.
Dos Santos and UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi exchanged notes last week, but the president insists the raid was against armed Hutu and Rwandan refugees in UNITA-held areas.
"There is no fighting going on because UNITA has no weapons and our soldiers are disarmed," UNITA's leader in parliament Abel Chivukuvuku told Reuters.
Angola's government had become impatient with UNITA's reluctance to share the diamond area, the only region out of government control.

U.N relief workers say thousands of people have fled the fighting and estimated 2,500 people had arrived in the government-held mining town of Nzage in the past week. The aid officials said those arriving report heavy fighting south of the town.
Diamond analysts say if the government continues its offensive toward UNITA's diamond stronghold at Lusamba, it could mean the end for the movement.
"If they lose Lusamba, it's all over for UNITA," said one analyst.
